h1: Football Matches Played in Extreme Weather
lead: Football is a winter sport played in the open, which means it has always been at the mercy of the elements. These are the matches that were played — or cancelled — in the most extreme weather imaginable.
thumbCaption: Football matches played in extreme weather
share: From the Big Freeze of 1963 to World Cups moved to avoid 40C heat — football's most extreme weather matches.
content:
Footballers play in rain, wind, sleet and frost as a matter of routine. Every winter brings a 'snow match' and every summer a heatwave. But occasionally the weather stops being a backdrop and becomes the story — the reason the game was abandoned, postponed or played in conditions that bordered on the absurd.

The Big Freeze of 1963

The most famous weather event in English football history is the winter of 1963, the coldest in the country for over two centuries. From late December to early March, snow and ice gripped Britain, and football shut down almost entirely:

  • FA Cup ties were postponed again and again, with some clubs waiting more than a month to play.
  • Bolton Wanderers went from December to February without playing a single competitive game.
  • The FA Cup final was pushed back to the end of May — the latest ever — and the whole season stretched four weeks beyond its normal finish.

The freeze had one lasting consequence: bookmakers had taken bets on football fixtures that were not being played, so the Pools Panel was created — a group of experts who 'decided' results of postponed matches so the pools could continue. The panel survived for decades.

The 2022 World Cup: Moving Football to Avoid the Heat

The ultimate example of football bending to extreme weather is the 2022 World Cup in Qatar. Qatar's summer temperatures regularly exceed 40C, which is dangerous for players and spectators, so FIFA made the unprecedented decision to move the tournament to November and December — the first World Cup ever played outside the traditional May-to-July window. Every stadium was air-conditioned, and matches kicked off in cooler evening temperatures. It was the largest weather-driven change in the history of international football.

The Snow Matches

Snow produces football's most beautiful photographs and some of its most memorable matches. A pitch covered in snow changes everything: passing becomes impossible, the ball stops dead, and games often descend into chaotic, mud-soaked battles decided by a single bounce.

Famous snow matches include the 'blizzard games' played across the United States and northern Europe, where officials have insisted the game continue despite visibility dropping to a few metres. In some of these matches, the pitch markings disappeared entirely and the lines had to be re-painted in yellow or the players simply played without them.

Monsoon and Torrential Rain

In tropical leagues, the monsoon season turns pitches into swimming pools, and a handful of matches have become legendary for being played in conditions closer to a water park than a football ground:

  • South Asian and South-East Asian leagues routinely reschedule around monsoon seasons, but flood matches still slip through.
  • In one famous European case, a Champions League game was played in such torrential rain that the pitch was covered in standing water and the ball stopped moving entirely mid-pass.

Extreme Heat at Sea Level

Heat affects football in ways snow cannot: it is a genuine health risk. FIFA introduced cooling breaks for tournaments played in hot conditions — a two-to-three minute break after the 30th minute of each half when temperatures become extreme, with the lost time added on as stoppage time. Those breaks, and the unusually long stoppage-time figures they create, have become a regular feature of summer tournaments.

The rule of thumb: Football is designed to be played in almost any weather, but only up to a point. Referees have the power to suspend matches for dangerous conditions — and across history, the extreme has rarely won the argument.

title: The Highest Altitude Football Stadiums in the World | WinFulltime
description: At 4,338 metres, Cerro de Pasco is the world's highest football stadium. Explore the highest altitude stadiums and the FIFA altitude rule.
keywords: highest football stadium, highest altitude football stadium, Cerro de Pasco 4338m, Hernando Siles La Paz, El Alto stadium, FIFA altitude ban, high altitude football
h1: The Highest Altitude Football Stadiums in the World
lead: Some football grounds sit more than 4,000 metres above sea level — so high that the ball flies further and visiting players struggle to breathe. These are the highest altitude football stadiums on Earth.
thumbCaption: The highest altitude football stadiums in the world
share: A FIFA-listed stadium at 4,338 metres, and an altitude rule FIFA tried to impose — the highest football grounds on Earth.
content:
Most of the world's football is played at sea level, where the ball behaves predictably and oxygen is plentiful. A handful of stadiums, almost all of them in the Andes, break every rule: they sit at altitudes that would floor an untrained tourist, and they give home teams one of the most famous unfair advantages in sport.

The Highest of Them All: Cerro de Pasco

The highest football stadium in the world is the Estadio Daniel Alcides Carrión in Cerro de Pasco, Peru, which sits at 4,338 metres above sea level — higher than the summit of most European mountains. The stadium has a capacity of around 12,000 and is listed by FIFA as the highest-altitude stadium in world football. The thin air at that altitude has two practical effects: the ball travels noticeably faster and further, and unacclimatised visiting players suffer. Cerro de Pasco's home advantage was once so extreme that away teams refused to play there, and even FIFA eventually got involved.

La Paz: Bolivia's Home Fortress

Bolivia plays its international matches at altitude, most famously at the Estadio Hernando Siles in La Paz, which sits at around 3,600 metres. With a capacity of over 41,000, it is one of the biggest and highest major stadiums in the world, opened in 1930 and expanded over the decades. Its record attendance was over 60,000.

La Paz's altitude has produced some of the most lopsided international results in history. Bolivia regularly beat far stronger South American sides at home, and visiting teams — especially from low-lying countries — complained that playing there was physically impossible. In 2010, Argentina were beaten in La Paz by a team they were vastly better than on paper, a result that made headlines worldwide.

El Alto: The Newest Extreme

In 2017, Bolivia opened the Estadio Municipal El Alto, a new ground at 4,088 metres — higher even than the Hernando Siles. Since 2024 the national team has played its home matches there, making Bolivia's internationals the highest-altitude fixtures in world football. At El Alto, players and fans routinely use oxygen masks in the stands, and visiting squads are given oxygen tanks on the bench.

FIFA's Attempt to Ban High-Altitude Football

The complaints about altitude grew so loud that FIFA tried to legislate against it. In May 2007, FIFA announced a ban on international matches played above 2,500 metres — a rule that would have stripped La Paz and other Andean stadiums of their international status. The decision provoked a furious reaction from Bolivia and the Andean nations, who argued it was an attack on their football.

Under political and sporting pressure, FIFA first raised the limit to 3,000 metres with an exception for La Paz, and then scrapped the ban entirely in May 2008. High-altitude football was officially legal again — and Cerro de Pasco, El Alto and La Paz kept their extraordinary home advantage.

StadiumCityAltitude
Daniel Alcides CarriónCerro de Pasco, Peru4,338 m
Estadio Municipal El AltoEl Alto, Bolivia4,088 m
Estadio Hernando SilesLa Paz, Bolivia~3,600 m
The altitude edge: At 4,000 metres the air holds about 40% less oxygen. Teams that live at altitude are unaffected; teams that arrive from sea level are not. That gap is the most extreme home advantage in world football.

title: The Lowest Attendance at a Major Football Match | WinFulltime
description: Wimbledon drew just 3,039 fans for a Premier League match against Everton in 1993. The lowest attendances ever recorded in major football.
keywords: lowest attendance football, lowest Premier League attendance, Wimbledon 3039, smallest crowd football league, empty stadium match, football attendance records
h1: The Lowest Attendance at a Major Football Match
lead: Some matches are played in front of 80,000 fans. A few famous ones were played in front of almost nobody. These are the lowest attendances ever recorded in major football.
thumbCaption: The lowest attendance at a major football match
share: 3,039 fans for a Premier League match — the lowest crowd ever recorded in England's top flight.
content:
Football is defined by its crowds. The sport's biggest matches pack 90,000 people into a stadium and broadcast to billions. But not every match is a sell-out, and a handful of fixtures have gone down in history for the opposite reason — the tiny, almost-empty grounds they were played in front of.

The Record: Wimbledon's 3,039

The lowest attendance ever recorded for a Premier League match is 3,039, set when Wimbledon hosted Everton at Selhurst Park on 26 January 1993. The match, which took place on a Tuesday night, drew a crowd smaller than many non-league games — and the figure has never been beaten since, even as the league has grown into the most watched in the world.

Why Was It So Empty?

Wimbledon's crowds were low for reasons that had nothing to do with quality. The club, originally from south London, shared Selhurst Park with Crystal Palace, meaning home fans watched their team play on another club's ground miles away. The 1992-93 season also saw Wimbledon struggle through a bleak midwinter run of fixtures, and a Tuesday night against mid-table Everton was not the fixture to fill the stands.

The result: an attendance so low that it became a trivia staple, and one that has resisted every challenge in the three decades since.

The Rest of the All-Time Low List

Wimbledon dominate the Premier League's all-time lowest-attendance list. The ten lowest crowds in the league's history were all Wimbledon home games in the 1992-93 and 1993-94 seasons, including:

AttendanceMatchDate
3,039Wimbledon vs EvertonJan 1993
3,386Oldham vs ...Dec 1992
3,759Coventry vs ...Aug 1992

Oldham Athletic's 3,386 and Coventry City's 3,759 are the famous near-misses — clubs whose big crowds at other grounds only made their empty nights more striking.

The 'Zero Attendance' Era

In the modern era, the lowest-attendance record was redefined in a different way. During the COVID-19 pandemic, leagues across the world played matches behind closed doors — with an official attendance of zero. The 2019-20 and 2020-21 seasons of the Premier League, La Liga and most of Europe's leagues were completed entirely in empty stadiums, meaning the 'lowest attendance' in football history, in a technical sense, is now zero.

Those matches are usually treated as a special case — nobody counts a pandemic lockdown as a genuine attendance record. But they prove a point: football can exist without a crowd, just not very well.

Why Low Crowds Matter

An empty stadium tells a story. It can signal a club in decline, a fixture nobody wants to see, or simply a club playing home games in the wrong place. Wimbledon's low crowds were a symptom of their ground-share; the club's subsequent relocation to Milton Keynes and the fans' rebellion that followed became one of the defining stories of English football's modern era.

The bottom line: The record-low Premier League attendance of 3,039, set by Wimbledon in January 1993, has stood for more than 30 years — and with the league's global popularity, it is unlikely ever to be beaten.

h1: The Most Watched Football Matches in History
lead: A football match can pull more viewers than the population of any country on Earth. These are the most watched football matches in history — headlined by a World Cup final that reached 1.5 billion people.
thumbCaption: The most watched football matches in history
share: 1.5 billion people watched the 2022 World Cup final. The most watched football matches in history, ranked.
content:
No other sport commands audiences like football. When the world's biggest matches kick off, they are watched not in hundreds of millions but in billions — more people than the population of Europe. The most watched football matches in history are almost all World Cup finals, and one of them stands alone.

The Record: The 2022 World Cup Final

The most watched football match in history is the 2022 World Cup final between Argentina and France in Qatar. An estimated 1.5 billion people watched the match, which saw Lionel Messi finally lift the trophy Argentina had waited 36 years for. The final drew 88,966 people to Lusail Stadium and a global television audience that made it the most viewed football match ever recorded.

The 2022 tournament as a whole reached an estimated 5 billion people across its month-long run — more than 60% of the planet — cementing the World Cup's status as the most watched sporting event on Earth.

The Other Giants

Behind the 2022 final, the biggest audiences in football history follow a clear pattern: World Cup finals and European finals dominate because they are the only matches watched by the entire planet at once.

MatchYearReported audience
World Cup final: Argentina vs France2022~1.5 billion
World Cup final: France vs Croatia2018~1.1 billion
World Cup final: Germany vs Argentina2014~1 billion
World Cup final: England vs West Germany1966~400 million (reported)
UEFA Champions League finalVarious350-450 million

Audience figures this large are estimates — no single measurement system covers the entire planet — but the ordering is beyond dispute. World Cup finals have been the most watched events in human history since television became global.

Why the Numbers Keep Growing

The growth is driven by one thing: reach. In 1966, the World Cup final was watched by a few hundred million people in black and white, mostly in Europe. By 2022, the final was broadcast in every country on Earth, on television, streaming and social media, in hundreds of languages. Football's audience does not replace itself — it adds whole continents.

The Club Match Records

Club football rarely competes with World Cup finals, but a few club fixtures have pulled genuinely enormous audiences:

  • El Clásico (Real Madrid vs Barcelona) is routinely described as the most watched club fixture in the world, with estimates of 500 million-plus for the biggest editions.
  • UEFA Champions League finals regularly reach 350 to 450 million viewers, making the final the most watched annual sporting event in the world.
  • The 2026 World Cup, hosted by the United States, Mexico and Canada, is expected to have set new records still being counted as broadcasters publish their figures.
The key number: The most watched football match in history is the 2022 World Cup final, with an audience of around 1.5 billion. It is the closest the sport has come to the entire human race watching the same ninety minutes at once.
